title: Cybersecurity Essentials
tagline: Protect your accounts, devices and data with habits that work, with practice in every module
summary: Learn practical cyber safety: the principles of security, strong passwords and two-step verification, spotting phishing and scams, securing devices and networks, backups, privacy and responding to incidents. This course is defensive and for everyday users. Every module has a hands-on lab.

modules.title: Security foundations
modules.summary: What we are protecting, who the attackers are and the basic principles of defence.
modules.outcome: You can describe confidentiality, integrity and availability, name common threats and explain defence in depth.
modules.intro: Cybersecurity is the practice of protecting people, devices and information from being stolen, damaged or misused. You do not need to be an engineer to defend yourself well. A handful of habits stop most attacks.

topics.title: The CIA triad
topics.html:
Three goals of security
PrincipleMeaningBroken by
ConfidentialityOnly authorised people can see the informationData theft, eavesdropping, shoulder surfing
IntegrityInformation is accurate and has not been alteredTampering, malware that edits files, forged documents
AvailabilitySystems and data are usable when neededOutages, ransomware, floods of traffic

Every security incident can be described by which of these it damages. A leaked list of student marks breaks confidentiality. A hacker changing the marks breaks integrity. A system that is offline on results day breaks availability.

Worked example

A school app

An app shows results to students.

  1. Confidentiality: each student sees only their own marks.
  2. Integrity: marks cannot be changed except by teachers, and changes are logged.
  3. Availability: the app works during results day, with enough capacity.

Answer. Good security designs for all three together.

Tip

When you hear about a security problem, ask which of the three it affects. It makes the news easier to understand.

Check what you just learned

1. Ransomware that locks files mainly attacks:
  • Confidentiality only
  • Integrity only
  • Availability (correct)
  • None

People cannot use their data.
keyPoints: Confidentiality, integrity and availability.
Describe incidents by which principle they break.

topics.title: Threats and attackers
topics.html:
Who might attack
TypeTypical goalExample
CriminalsMoneyFake bank messages, ransomware
OpportunistsWhatever is easyGuessing weak passwords
InsidersRevenge or gain, or sometimes accidentsA staff member copying data
ActivistsPublicityDefacing a website
State-backed groupsSpying or disruptionTargeting governments and companies
Common threats
ThreatWhat it is
MalwareHarmful software: viruses, ransomware, spyware
PhishingFake messages that trick you into giving away information
Credential stuffingTrying stolen passwords on other sites
Social engineeringManipulating people rather than machines
Data breachUnauthorised access to stored data
Denial of serviceOverloading a service so people cannot use it

Most attacks on ordinary people are not clever. They rely on reused passwords, urgent messages and out-of-date software. This is good news: basic habits block most of them.

Watch out

This course is about defence. Never attempt to access systems or accounts that you do not own or are not authorised to test; it is illegal in most countries.

Check what you just learned

1. Phishing is:
  • A fishing sport
  • A backup
  • A kind of firewall
  • Fake messages that trick people (correct)

It exploits trust.
keyPoints: Attackers range from opportunists to organised criminals.
Most attacks exploit common weaknesses, not genius.

topics.title: Defence in depth
topics.html:
Definition

Defence in depth. Using several layers of protection, so that if one fails, others still stand in the way. No single control is perfect.

Layers of defence
LayerExamples
PeopleAwareness, good habits, reporting
AccountsStrong passwords, two-step verification
DevicesUpdates, screen lock, antivirus, encryption
NetworkSecure wifi, HTTPS, firewalls
DataBackups, encryption, limited sharing
ResponseA plan for when something goes wrong

Principles

  • Least privilege: give people and apps only the access they need.
  • Keep it simple: complexity breeds mistakes.
  • Assume you will be breached sometime and prepare to recover.
  • Fail safely: when something breaks, default to closed.

A common home example: a good lock, an alarm, a neighbour who watches and an insurance policy. Each is imperfect, but together they make a burglar's job hard and the loss recoverable.

Check what you just learned

1. Defence in depth means:
  • Several layers of protection (correct)
  • One strong lock
  • No protection
  • Hiding

Redundancy protects.

Key terms: flip and sort

Confidentiality
Only the right people can see data
Integrity
Data is accurate and unaltered
Availability
Systems work when needed
Malware
Harmful software
Least privilege
Only the access that is needed
keyPoints: Layer defences; no single control is enough.
Use least privilege and plan for recovery.

modules.title: Passwords and accounts
modules.summary: Create strong passwords, use a manager, turn on two-step verification and protect your main accounts.
modules.outcome: You can explain why length matters, build a passphrase, use a password manager and protect an email account.
modules.intro: Your email account is the key to your digital life, because password resets go there. Protecting it, and the passwords you use, is the most valuable security habit you can build.

topics.title: What makes a password strong
topics.html:
Attackers do not usually guess one password at a time by hand. They use software that can try millions or billions of guesses a second against stolen data. What matters is how many guesses it would take.

Formula · Possible passwords

possibilities = (size of the character set) ^ (length)

8 lowercase letters: 26^8 is about 209 billion. 12 lowercase letters: 26^12 is about 95 quadrillion, almost half a million times more.

Length versus complexity

Change the character set and length to see how many possibilities exist and how long a billion-guesses-a-second attacker would need in days.

Adjust Character set size, Length and see Possibilities, Days to try everything at 1 billion a second change.

What really helps
HabitWhy
Length (12+ characters)Each extra character multiplies the work
Unrelated words in a passphraseEasy to remember, hard to guess
Never reusing passwordsOne breach does not open other accounts
Avoiding personal detailsNames and birthdays are guessed first
Tip

A passphrase such as four random, unrelated words is both stronger and easier to remember than a short password full of symbols.

Check what you just learned

1. Which is generally stronger?
  • A short password with symbols
  • A long passphrase of random words (correct)
  • Your birthday
  • Your name

Length multiplies the work.
keyPoints: Length and uniqueness matter most.
Use a passphrase of unrelated words.

topics.title: Password managers and two-step verification
topics.html:
No one can remember dozens of unique, long passwords. A password manager stores them encrypted behind one strong master passphrase and fills them in for you.

What a manager does
FeatureBenefit
Generates random passwordsUnique and strong for each site
Fills only on the right websiteHelps avoid fake login pages
Syncs across devicesConvenience
Warns about breaches and reuseQuick fixes
Definition

Two-step verification. A second proof of identity after your password, such as a code from an app, a hardware key or a prompt on your phone. A stolen password alone is no longer enough.

Second step options
OptionStrength
Hardware security keyVery strong, resists phishing
Authenticator app codeStrong
Prompt in a trusted appStrong, watch for approving by accident
SMS codeBetter than nothing, but vulnerable to SIM swap and interception
Watch out

Never share a verification code with anyone. A real company will never ask for it.

Check what you just learned

1. A real company asking you for your one-time code is:
  • Normal
  • Required
  • A warning sign (correct)
  • Polite

Never share codes.
keyPoints: A password manager gives you unique, strong passwords.
Two-step verification stops stolen passwords working alone.

topics.title: Protecting your main accounts
topics.html:
Priority order

  1. 1. Your main email: it resets everything else.
  2. 2. Banking and payment accounts.
  3. 3. Your phone account and app store.
  4. 4. Social media and messaging.
  5. 5. Shopping and other accounts.
Account hygiene
TaskHow often
Check recovery email and phone numbersEvery few months
Review connected apps and devicesEvery few months
Remove unused accountsYearly
Check whether your email appears in a known breachWhen news appears, or twice a year

Common mistakes

  • Using the same password for email and everything else.
  • Answering security questions truthfully when the answers can be found online.
  • Leaving accounts logged in on shared computers.
  • Ignoring login alerts.
Tip

Treat 'security questions' as extra passwords. Make up answers and store them in your password manager.

Think of your email address as the master key to a building full of rooms. A shopping site, a social network and a bank may each keep their own lock, but all of them will open a door for whoever can read your email, because every 'forgot password' link is sent there. This is why security advisers repeat the same advice about email so often: a unique long passphrase, two-step verification with an authenticator app or a hardware key, and a regular check of which devices and apps are signed in. Fifteen minutes spent on email protects more than hours spent on any other single account.

Check what you just learned

1. Which account should you secure first?
  • A game
  • A quiz site
  • A shopping site
  • Your main email (correct)

It resets the others.

Key terms: flip and sort

Passphrase
A long password made of several words
Password manager
An encrypted store of passwords
Two-step verification
A second proof of identity
Credential stuffing
Trying leaked passwords on other sites
Recovery email
The address used to reset an account
keyPoints: Protect email first; check recovery options and logins.
Treat security questions as passwords.

modules.title: Phishing and social engineering
modules.summary: Recognise manipulation by message, call and site, and respond safely.
modules.outcome: You can spot phishing signs, handle suspicious calls and links and report incidents.
modules.intro: The easiest way into a system is often through a person. Social engineering uses trust, curiosity, fear and urgency. The defence is a calm pause.

topics.title: How phishing works
topics.html:
Warning signs
SignExample
Urgency or threatsYour account will close in one hour
Look-alike addressesbank-security@secure-b4nk.example
Generic greetingDear customer
Unexpected attachment or linkinvoice.exe, shortened links
Requests for secretsPassword, OTP, PIN
Too good to be trueYou have won a prize
Poor languageNot always: good fakes exist

What to do instead

  • Pause. Do not click.
  • Go to the official site or app yourself, not through the link.
  • Call the official number printed on your card or website.
  • Report the message.
  • If you already clicked and typed a password, change it at once.
Tip

The calmer you are, the harder you are to trick. Attackers want you rushed.

Phishing messages are getting better, and a good habit is more reliable than trying to spot every flaw. Treat any message that asks you to log in, pay, or share a code as unverified until you check by another route. If an email says your delivery failed, open the courier's own app. If a message says your bank account has a problem, call the number on the back of your card. This habit costs thirty seconds and defeats even excellent forgeries, because the attacker cannot control the route you choose for the second check.

It also helps to remember that attackers research their targets. A message that mentions your real teacher, your real college or a purchase you actually made may come from someone who has gathered that detail from public profiles or an earlier data leak. This is called spear phishing. The existence of a correct personal detail is therefore not proof that a message is genuine. Judge the request itself: is it asking for a password, money, a code, or for you to install something? If yes, verify independently, however convincing the detail.

Check what you just learned

1. A message demands action in one hour. This is:
  • A warning sign (correct)
  • Normal
  • A guarantee
  • Required

Urgency is a standard trick.
keyPoints: Phishing copies trusted brands and creates urgency.
Go to the official site yourself; never use the link.

topics.title: Calls, messages and fake support
topics.html:
Common scams
ScamHow it worksDefence
Fake bank callCaller says there is fraud and asks for OTP or PINHang up; call the official number yourself
Tech support scamCaller says your computer is infected; asks for remote accessReal companies do not call unasked; never give remote access
Prize or lotteryPay a fee to claimYou cannot win a contest you did not enter
Romance or investment scamA new online friend recommends a schemeNever send money to someone you have not met
Delivery textA link for a small feeUse the courier's app or site
Job scamPay to get hired or process payments for 'employer'Genuine employers never charge candidates

These scams rely on emotion: fear, greed, loneliness or curiosity. Learn the pattern and you will recognise new versions.

Watch out

If you have lost money, contact your bank immediately and report to your national cybercrime authority. Speed matters. Do not feel ashamed: skilled criminals deceive intelligent people every day.

Check what you just learned

1. A caller from 'your bank' asks for your OTP. You should:
  • Give it
  • Hang up and call the official number (correct)
  • Give half
  • Ask for their ID

Banks never ask for it.
keyPoints: Hang up and call the official number yourself.
Never pay to receive a prize or a job.

topics.title: Staying safe online and reporting
topics.html:
Link and attachment checks

  • Hover over (or long-press) a link to see where it really goes.
  • Check the website name carefully for small changes.
  • Look for HTTPS, but remember that criminals use it too.
  • Do not open unexpected attachments, especially executable files.
  • When in doubt, ask the sender through another channel.
Report where
WhereTo whom
At work or schoolThe IT or security team
On a platformThe platform's report button
Fraud involving moneyYour bank, then the cybercrime authority
A lost or stolen deviceYour phone company and employer

Reporting helps others. A message that reaches you has probably reached many more, and a quick report lets the team block it.

Tip

Take a screenshot of the scam message before you delete it, and write down the sender and time.

Check what you just learned

1. Reporting a scam message helps:
  • Nobody
  • The scammer
  • Others avoid it (correct)
  • Only you

It protects the community.

Key terms: flip and sort

Phishing
Fake messages to steal information
Social engineering
Manipulating people
OTP
One-time password
Remote access
Control of your device from afar
Spoofing
Faking a sender's identity
keyPoints: Check links before clicking; use another channel to verify.
Report scams to protect others.

modules.title: Devices, networks and data
modules.summary: Keep devices updated and locked, use networks safely and protect data with backups and encryption.
modules.outcome: You can secure a phone and laptop, use public wifi safely and plan backups with the 3-2-1 rule.
modules.intro: Your devices hold your photos, messages and banking apps. A few settings make them far harder to compromise and far easier to recover.

topics.title: Securing your devices
topics.html:
The essentials

  1. Turn on automatic updates for the system and apps.
  2. Use a screen lock with a PIN of at least six digits, or a password or biometric.
  3. Enable device encryption (often on by default).
  4. Turn on 'find my device' and remote wipe.
  5. Install apps only from official stores and review permissions.
  6. Remove apps you no longer use.
Why updates matter
Without updatesWith updates
Known vulnerabilities stay openFixes are installed quickly
Attackers use public exploitsExploits stop working
Apps may be unstableBetter stability and features
Watch out

Be careful with 'cracked' software, unofficial app stores and unknown USB sticks. They are common ways to deliver malware.

Tip

If your device is lost, a screen lock and encryption stop the finder from reading your data, and remote wipe lets you erase it.

Check what you just learned

1. Why install updates promptly?
  • They are optional
  • They use more data
  • They remove apps
  • They close known security holes (correct)

Attackers target known flaws.
keyPoints: Updates, screen lock, encryption and find-my-device.
Use official stores and review permissions.

topics.title: Safe networking
topics.html:
Home and public networks
SettingAdvice
Home routerChange the default admin password; use WPA2 or WPA3; update firmware
Guest networkUse it for visitors and smart devices
Public wifiTreat as untrusted; avoid sensitive accounts, or use mobile data
VPNEncrypts traffic between you and the VPN provider; choose a reputable provider and know it does not make you anonymous
HTTPSPadlock means the connection is encrypted, not that the site is trustworthy

On public wifi

  • Prefer your phone's mobile data for banking.
  • Turn off automatic joining of open networks.
  • Check the exact network name with staff.
  • Log out and 'forget' the network afterwards.
  • Heed certificate warnings: do not continue past them.

A fake hotspot named like a real one can be set up in minutes, so a strange network name in a cafe is a reason for care.

Check what you just learned

1. A padlock in the browser means:
  • The connection is encrypted (correct)
  • The site is trustworthy
  • The site is government-run
  • No malware

Encryption only.
keyPoints: Secure the router; treat public wifi as untrusted.
HTTPS shows encryption, not trustworthiness.

topics.title: Protecting your data: backups and encryption
topics.html:
Definition

The 3-2-1 backup rule. Keep at least 3 copies of your data, on 2 different types of storage, with 1 copy off-site (such as a cloud service or a drive at another location).

Why it works
RiskWhich copy saves you
Laptop stolenExternal drive or cloud
Disk failsAnother copy
Fire or flood at homeOff-site copy
Ransomware encrypts live filesAn offline or versioned backup

Backup habits

  • Back up automatically.
  • Test restoring a file now and then.
  • Keep one backup disconnected from the computer.
  • Encrypt backups that hold sensitive data.
Tip

A backup you have never tested is a hope, not a backup.

Check what you just learned

1. In the 3-2-1 rule the '1' stands for:
  • One password
  • One off-site copy (correct)
  • One virus
  • One disk

Protection from local disasters.

Key terms: flip and sort

Update
A new version that fixes problems
Encryption
Scrambling data so only authorised people can read it
VPN
A virtual private network
Backup
A spare copy of data
Ransomware
Malware that locks data for payment
keyPoints: 3 copies, 2 types of storage, 1 off-site.
Test your restores.

practical.title: Practical: a device check
steps: Test restoring one photo from a backup.

options: A six-digit PIN or longer, or a password

modules.title: Risk and privacy
modules.summary: Think about risk systematically and protect your personal information.
modules.outcome: You can score and rank personal security risks, explain what personal data is and set privacy controls.
modules.intro: You cannot defend against everything. Thinking about risk helps you decide what to fix first. Privacy is the related skill of deciding what to share, with whom.

topics.title: Thinking about risk
topics.html:
Formula · Risk score

risk = likelihood × impact

A reused password is very likely to be attacked (5) and would be very damaging (4): score 20.

Responses to a risk
ResponseExample
ReduceTurn on two-step verification
AvoidStop using an unsafe app
TransferInsurance; using a bank that refunds fraud
AcceptAccept a small risk, such as an old unused account, knowingly
Tip

Fix the highest scores first. A few cheap actions remove most of your risk.

Check what you just learned

1. A risk with likelihood 4 and impact 5 scores:
  • 9
  • 1
  • 20 (correct)
  • 45

4 × 5 = 20.
keyPoints: Risk is likelihood times impact.
Fix the highest risks first.

topics.title: Personal data and privacy
topics.html:
Definition

Personal data. Any information that can identify you or relate to you: name, phone, address, ID numbers, photos, location, online identifiers and health information.

Sensitivity
LevelExamplesCare
LowFavourite filmShare freely
MediumSchool name, cityThink about context
HighID numbers, bank details, passwords, health recordsProtect strongly; share only when really needed

Privacy habits

  • Review privacy settings on social media.
  • Limit app permissions (location, camera, contacts).
  • Share the minimum needed in forms.
  • Think before posting photos with background details.
  • Use separate email addresses for different purposes.
  • Read what a service does with your data before agreeing.

Laws in many countries give you rights over your data: to know what is held, to correct it and sometimes to have it deleted. Check the laws and the company's privacy policy where you live.

Check what you just learned

1. A form asks for more data than needed. You should:
  • Fill everything
  • Never use forms
  • Lie about everything
  • Share only what is necessary (correct)

Data minimisation.
keyPoints: Share the minimum; review settings and permissions.
Know your rights over your data.

topics.title: Children, family and safe sharing
topics.html:
Digital safety is a family matter. Younger people and older adults are both targeted, in different ways.

Tips by group
GroupTips
Children and teensTalk openly, set privacy, teach them to tell an adult about anything uncomfortable, and avoid sharing school and location details
Older adultsTeach scam patterns, help set up two-step verification, and agree a code word for emergencies
EveryoneAgree that anyone can ask 'is this a scam?' without embarrassment

Healthy habits at home

  • Keep devices in shared spaces for younger children.
  • Use parental controls as support, not as a substitute for conversation.
  • Back up family photos.
  • Use a shared password manager for family accounts if suitable.
Watch out

If a child or anyone experiences bullying, threats or exploitation online, save the evidence, report it to the platform and tell a trusted adult or the relevant authority.

Check what you just learned

1. The best protection for children online is:
  • Open conversation and settings (correct)
  • Silence
  • Ignoring it
  • Sharing everything

Trust and settings work together.

Key terms: flip and sort

Risk
Likelihood times impact
Personal data
Information relating to a person
Data minimisation
Collecting only what is needed
Privacy settings
Controls over who sees your data
keyPoints: Talk openly with children and older relatives.
Report bullying and threats; keep evidence.

practical.title: Practical: a privacy audit
steps: Remove one old post or app.

options: Limited to what the app needs
Saving evidence and telling a trusted adult
Give you rights over your data in many places

modules.title: When things go wrong
modules.summary: Respond calmly to a hacked account, lost device or scam, and keep improving.
modules.outcome: You can follow a simple response plan, report incidents properly and learn from them.
modules.intro: However careful you are, something may go wrong. People who respond quickly and calmly lose far less than those who panic or hide it.

topics.title: A simple response plan
topics.html:
Scenario: hacked account
StepActions
StopChange the password from a safe device; sign out all sessions
RecoverTurn on two-step verification; check recovery email, phone, forwarding rules and connected apps
TellWarn contacts; report to the service; inform the bank if money is involved
LearnHow did it happen? Reused password? Fake login page? Fix that
Scenario: lost phone
StepActions
StopLock or erase the phone remotely; call your mobile provider to block the SIM
RecoverRestore from backup on a new device; change important passwords
TellInform your bank and employer or school if needed
LearnEnable screen lock, encryption, backups
Tip

Write your response plan now and keep a copy offline. In a crisis you will not think clearly.

Check what you just learned

1. The first step after a hacked account is to:
  • Wait
  • Stop the damage (correct)
  • Post online
  • Delete everything

Contain it quickly.
keyPoints: Stop, recover, tell, learn.
Write your plan before you need it.

topics.title: Reporting and getting help
topics.html:
What to record

  • What happened and when.
  • What accounts or devices are involved.
  • Screenshots and messages.
  • What you did in response.
  • Money lost, if any.
Who to contact
SituationContact
Money lostYour bank at once, then the cybercrime authority
Identity theftLocal police or cybercrime authority; credit agencies where relevant
Work or school accountsThe IT or security team
HarassmentThe platform and, where needed, the police
Child safety concernTrusted adult, platform, child-protection helplines
Watch out

Do not pay a ransom or a scammer's 'recovery fee'. Paying seldom returns your data and may attract more attacks. Seek proper help.

People are often embarrassed. Please do not be. Reporting quickly is a sign of good judgement and may prevent others from being hurt.

Check what you just learned

1. If you lose money to a scam you should:
  • Hide it
  • Pay more to recover it
  • Contact your bank at once (correct)
  • Wait a month

Time may help recover funds.
keyPoints: Record facts, report to the right place, and avoid paying scammers.
Speed matters; embarrassment does not.

topics.title: Building a security habit
topics.html:
A simple yearly rhythm
WhenDo
MonthlyCheck updates and review login alerts
Every few monthsReview recovery options and connected apps
Twice a yearTest a restore from backup; check for breaches
After any incidentUpdate your plan

Stay informed

  • Follow your national cybersecurity agency's advice.
  • Read the security notices from your bank and main services.
  • Share what you learn with family and friends.
  • Be sceptical of dramatic news and check it before sharing.

Good security is not a one-time project. It is a few habits repeated, like brushing your teeth. The goal is not perfect safety but being a harder target than the next person, and being able to recover when something happens.

Tip

Make it social. Agree with friends or family that anyone may ask 'is this a scam?' and nobody will be judged.

Check what you just learned

1. Security is best treated as:
  • A one-off project
  • A product to buy
  • Impossible
  • An ongoing habit (correct)

Repeated small actions.

Key terms: flip and sort

Incident
A security event needing a response
Containment
Stopping the damage
Recovery
Restoring access and data
Lessons learned
Changes made after an incident
keyPoints: Small recurring habits beat big one-off efforts.
Share knowledge and ask for help without shame.

Share it with a family member.
